chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Yahya ibn Imran al-Halabi, from Mu'alla ibn Uthman, from Ali ibn Hanzala, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:
The happy one is made to travel along the path of the miserable until the people say: How he resembles them! Nay, he is of them. Then happiness overtakes him.
And the miserable one may be made to travel along the path of the happy ones until the people say: How he resembles them! Nay, he is of them. Then misery overtakes him.
Verily, the one whom God has decreed as happy — even if nothing remains of the world except the duration of milking a she-camel — He will seal his end with happiness.

key_terms.الأشقياء: The miserable/wretched ones (ashqiya') — those decreed for misery
key_terms.السعيد: The happy/fortunate one (sa'id) — one destined for happiness in the divine decree
key_terms.فواق ناقة: Duration of milking a she-camel — a proverbial expression for an extremely brief span of time
key_terms.كتبه الله: God has written/decreed — the concept of divine predetermination of one's ultimate fate
key_terms.يتداركه: Overtakes/rectifies him — divine destiny catching up to a person despite appearances

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about divine predetermination of happiness and misery in al-Kafi?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches about the concept of divine decree regarding happiness (sa'ada) and misery (shaqa'). He describes how appearances are deceptive — a destined fortunate person may temporarily walk among the wretched, and vice versa — but ultimately, divine predetermination prevails. The hadith concludes with the striking guarantee that one decreed by God to be happy will end in happiness no matter how brief his remaining worldly life. This teaching addresses the perennial question of human destiny, appearing in the chapter on happiness and misery in al-Kafi, providing theological grounding for trust in God's ultimate justice and the finality of one's destined end.
